links.note: The Council of Chalcedon deposed Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, in October 451. A petition quoted by the historian Evagrius says Timothy Aelurus broke from the church right after the council. John of Ephesus, writing for the other side, says Justinian drove Patriarch Theodosius from his throne for refusing Chalcedon.

prose_changes.old: Continues Alexandria + Desert; contested sibling of the Chalcedonian and Syriac Orthodox traditions

prose_changes.old: This is one of the traditions on the map that never ended: the same institution continued under Muslim rule as Coptic Christianity, and its patriarchal line runs unbroken to the Coptic Orthodox pope of Alexandria today. It gave the wider Oriental Orthodox family — Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian, Eritrean — its shared theological anchor in Cyril of Alexandria, and it made Coptic a liturgical language still sung in Egyptian churches every week. Its desert monasteries in the Wadi Natrun and its painted late-antique churches in Upper Egypt are still standing, and most are still in use.

prose_changes.old: Christianity reached the Nubian kingdoms south of Egypt through competing missions in the 540s — a Miaphysite priest named Julian sent with the empress Theodora's backing, and a Chalcedonian effort sent with Justinian's. And the story of that race survives only because a Syrian bishop, John of Ephesus, wrote it down from the winning side. What Nubia itself left is not narrative but walls. The cathedral at Faras, built a few generations later,, buried in sand and rescued before the Aswan dam flooded the region, gave up a list of its bishops and more than a hundred painted figures: Nubian bishops, kings and queens, saints, some with dark faces and some pale, in a style nobody had seen before. When Arab armies pushed south after taking Egypt, Nubian archers held them at Dongola, and in 652 the two sides signed the Baqt. A treaty of exchange rather than of conquest, which left Christian Nubia standing on its own terms.

prose_changes.old: Aksum had been Christian since the fourth century, and in the period after Chalcedon it was a serious Red Sea power with its own coinage, its own script, and its Bible being translated into Ge'ez. Tradition credits the spread of monasticism and much of that translation work to the Nine Saints, monks said to have come from the Roman east around the turn of the sixth century. In 523 the Jewish king of Himyar, across the water in Yemen, massacred the Christians of Najran. The Aksumite king Kaleb crossed the Red Sea in about 525, destroyed his kingdom, and for a few decades Aksum ruled southern Arabia. Its church stayed in communion with Alexandria and shared its refusal of Chalcedon. Evidence from inside this particular window is thin — inscriptions, a few very early gospel books, archaeology. But the kingdom was still substantial enough in 615 that Muhammad sent his first followers to its king for protection.
prose_changes.new: Aksum had been Christian since the fourth century. In the period after Chalcedon it was a serious Red Sea power, with its own coinage, its own script, and its Bible being translated into Ge'ez. Tradition credits the spread of monasticism and much of that translation work to the Nine Saints. They are said to have been monks from the Roman east, arriving around the turn of the sixth century. In 523 the Jewish king of Himyar, across the water in Yemen, massacred the Christians of Najran. The Aksumite king Kaleb crossed the Red Sea in about 525, killed him, and set up a Christian king who paid Aksum tribute. Not long after, the Aksumite soldiers who had stayed behind set up another king, Abramus, and Aksum could not remove him. A Miaphysite historian of the time counted the Aksumite king as a fellow believer. No text from inside these years shows where its church stood on Chalcedon. Evidence from this window is thin: inscriptions, a few very early gospel books, archaeology. Muslim tradition remembers that around 615 Muhammad sent his first followers to its king for protection.
prose_changes.reason: Three changes. (1) 'Destroyed his kingdom, and for a few decades Aksum ruled southern Arabia': Procopius (Wars I.20, lines 2586-2626) says Kaleb killed the king and set up a tributary Christian king, who was soon overthrown by Abramus, whom Aksum failed to remove. (2) 'Stayed in communion with Alexandria and shared its refusal of Chalcedon': not shown by any vendored text of the window; restated as John of Ephesus's 'he also was a believer'. (3) Muhammad's followers in 615: no vendored or repo-cited source; attributed to Muslim tradition (see wants). Long sentences split.

Its church stayed in communion with Alexandria and shared its rejection of Chalcedon, though the direct evidence from these particular centuries is thin: mostly inscriptions, early manuscripts and archaeology.

prose_changes.reason: 'Briefly ruled southern Arabia' and 'stayed in communion with Alexandria and shared its rejection of Chalcedon' qualified as in the longDescription (Procopius, Wars I.20; John of Ephesus, Lives, Simeon). The text's own statement that the evidence is thin is kept.

prose_changes.old: The Nicene church of Roman Africa, restored after a century of Vandal persecution, was heir to the earlier African Christian tradition of Tertullian, Cyprian and Augustine, and became one of the principal voices resisting Justinian's condemnation of the Three Chapters.
prose_changes.new: The Nicene church of Roman Africa, restored after nearly a century of Vandal rule and repeated persecution. Its bishops still cited Cyprian and Augustine, great teachers of the earlier African church that had also produced Tertullian. It became one of the principal voices resisting Justinian's condemnation of the Three Chapters.
prose_changes.reason: 'Heir to the tradition of Tertullian': no text shows this church using Tertullian; Facundus cites Cyprian and Augustine (Pro def. I.3, I.4). 'A century of Vandal persecution': Vandal rule ran from the 430s to 533, but persecution came in waves; Procopius says Hilderic (523) was harsh 'neither to the Christians nor to anyone else' (Wars III.9, lines 1028-1031). Restated to match.

prose_changes.old: When Belisarius destroyed the Vandal kingdom in 533, the Nicene church of Roman Africa came out of a century of persecution and was restored to its buildings and its bishoprics. And within twenty years it was the most stubborn opposition Justinian faced anywhere in his own empire. When he condemned the Three Chapters to appease the Miaphysites, the African bishops refused. Facundus of Hermiane wrote twelve books against it, Reparatus of Carthage was deposed and exiled, and the chronicler Victor of Tunnuna spent years in prison and exile for the same refusal. Africa stayed a place where theology got argued at full volume. Maximus the Confessor spent formative years here, and African councils in 646 rejected the empire's next attempted compromise about the wills of Christ. Then Arab armies reached Carthage in the 690s, and the ancient African church, the church that had given Latin Christianity Tertullian, Cyprian and Augustine, was finished within a few generations.
prose_changes.new: When Belisarius destroyed the Vandal kingdom in 533, the Nicene church of Roman Africa came out of nearly a century of Vandal rule and repeated persecution. It was restored to its buildings and its bishoprics. Within twenty years it was among the most stubborn opposition Justinian faced anywhere in his own empire. When he condemned the Three Chapters to appease the Miaphysites, the African bishops refused. Facundus of Hermiane wrote twelve books against it, Reparatus of Carthage was deposed and exiled, and the chronicler Victor of Tunnuna spent years in prison and exile for the same refusal. Africa stayed a place where theology got argued at full volume. Maximus the Confessor lived here for some years, and in 645 he debated the deposed patriarch Pyrrhus in Africa. African councils in 646 rejected the empire's next attempted compromise about the wills of Christ. Then Arab armies reached Carthage in the 690s. The ancient African church, which had given Latin Christianity Tertullian, Cyprian and Augustine, was finished within a few generations.
prose_changes.reason: Three changes. (1) 'A century of persecution' as in the relationsSummary. (2) 'The most stubborn opposition Justinian faced anywhere': Victor of Tunnuna also records an Illyrian synod defending the Three Chapters (s.a. 549, Mommsen line 19038), so 'among the most stubborn'. (3) 'Maximus spent formative years here': he came to Africa as an adult monk; what the vendored text shows is the disputation with Pyrrhus held in Africa (PG 91, the Acta disputationis, lines ~15042-15063; date 645 from the file header). Long sentences split; every other fact kept.

prose_changes.old: This church left no successor. Latin Christianity in North Africa dwindled after the conquest and had effectively disappeared by the later Middle Ages — the only major region of the ancient Christian world to vanish so completely. But it handed on its refusal. Its resistance over the Three Chapters hardened a Western conviction that an emperor could not settle doctrine by decree, and its part in the argument over Christ's wills fed straight into the council of 680-681 that closed it. Its earlier centuries had already given the Latin church Tertullian, Cyprian and Augustine; what this last century added was a demonstration that a provincial church could tell an empire no. The ruins of Carthage and of dozens of African basilicas remain.
prose_changes.new: This church left no successor. Latin Christianity in North Africa dwindled after the conquest and had effectively disappeared by the later Middle Ages. It is the only major region of the ancient Christian world to vanish so completely. But it handed on its refusal. Its bishops wrote to the emperor in defence of writings the council of Chalcedon had accepted, and would not condemn them. In 646 its councils wrote to Rome against the teaching of a single will in Christ, and their letters were read out at the Roman synod of 649. The council of 680-681 later condemned that teaching. Its earlier centuries had already given the Latin church Tertullian, Cyprian and Augustine. What this last century added was a demonstration that a provincial church could tell an empire no. The ruins of Carthage and of dozens of African basilicas remain.
prose_changes.reason: Two reception claims qualified. (1) 'Hardened a Western conviction that an emperor could not settle doctrine by decree': no vendored text shows that reception; restated as what Facundus (preface, to Justinian) and Victor of Tunnuna (s.a. 550) show. (2) 'Fed straight into the council of 680-681 that closed it': the vendored chain is the 646 letters read at the Lateran synod of 649 (Mansi X, lines 93425-93430) and Constantinople III's two-wills definition (NPNF 2.14, line 24884); restated as that sequence without the causal 'straight into'. Long sentences split; every other fact kept.
